newsitem.title: DUBAI: MIDEAST GULF OIL OUTLOOK - IRAQ DAMPENS RECOVERY.
newsitem.headline: MIDEAST GULF OIL OUTLOOK - IRAQ DAMPENS RECOVERY.

text.p: Oil tankers loading crude at Iraq's Mina al-Bakr export terminal under the United Nations "oil-for-food" deal are expected to dominate both Gulf product and crude markets next week, Gulf traders said.
Tankers are due to arrive at the terminal in the northern Gulf in the coming week, marking Iraq's first crude exports from the Gulf since the last U.N. sales period expired in June.
Shipping sources in the region on Thursday said that there were no signs yet of tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz on route to al-Bakr, 12 miles (19 km) off Iraq's southern Fao Peninsula.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed on Wednesday told a news conference that Baghdad expected to resume oil exports in the middle of August.
But some traders expect first shipments from al-Bakr or Ceyhan as early as August 10 if sales contracts can be agreed and signed.

American, Russian, Japanese and Indian firms are expected to be among the first wave of lifters of Iraq's Basrah Light grade from al-Bakr which exported an average of 270,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first phase of the deal which ran from December 1996 to June this year.

Gulf traders expect Iraq to attempt to sell approximately double the amount from al-Bakr in the first 90-day period of the sale which ends September 5 and continue strong export flows in the subsequent 90-day period ending December 6.
U.S. independent firm Bayoil has been tipped as the first company to take a tanker to the terminal though tanker market sources said that final ship fixtures had not been made.

Gulf crude premiums for end September and October cargoes are expected to come under sustained pressure on the return of Iraqi oil though premiums for the remaining September cargoes are expected to be largely resilient.
Spot market premiums to official selling prices (OSP) for Abu Dhabi, Omani and Qatari grades loading in September have staged a strong recovery since early July.

Major producers Saudi Arabia, Iran and Kuwait will also have to keep a close eye on Iraq's reemergence as a marketing force in the Gulf if Baghdad makes major in-roads into lucrative Japanese and other key Asian markets.
Rasheed told reporters that Iraq's total crude export capacity stood at 1.8 million bpd though did not give separate figures for Ceyhan and al-Bakr.
Gulf-based traders estimate that al-Bakr could handle approximately one million bpd if necessary but doubts remain over the operational capability and safety of the port.
Murban has chalked up a 5-10 cents premium to the ADNOC OSP, recovering from a 30 cents discount at the start of the month to reach its highest premium since February.
"Gulf cargoes could be in for a rocky time for the rest of the year if Iraq turns on the tap," said one Gulf-based trader.

Middle distillates in the Gulf held up on firm European and Singapore markets, tighter August supplies and regional refinery maintenance despite a disappointing diesel tender purchase by Indian Oil Corp (IOC).
"The (products) market here will have little momentum of its own. Everything will link back to how futures will react to Iraq," a trader said.
